claim: Generic awareness or 'be unbiased' instructions give small, uneven and sometimes negative effects on LLM bias; the sign depends on model and bias type.
agent_test: Run a plain model with and without a one-line awareness prompt on paired biased/neutral items for 3 bias types; count items changed, equal tokens.

claim: A debiasing instruction can backfire on judgment-type biases (accuracy -4.4 points on average across three models; per-bias drops of 13 to 21 points) while fixing position-type response bias (+40.5).
agent_test: Replicate per bias: instruction vs none on 10 judgment biases, report signed deltas, equal tokens.

claim: Telling a model to ignore an anchor does not reduce anchoring; chain of thought, principles and reflection also fail.
agent_test: Anchored numeric estimates: plain vs ignore-the-anchor vs CoT; compare anchoring index.
audit_note: Minor: Lou and Sun test mostly GPT-4/GPT-4o (GPT-3.5 varied), and SynAnchors reports one method (Anti-DP) that lowers Llama anchoring 34.7 to 24.7, so 'fail' means simple prompt strategies.

claim: Rewriting the biasing text with a model-run loop cuts measured bias when the cue is planted in the text: the iterated SACD loop beat vanilla, CoT and self-help in every domain by its third round, and one-pass self-help worked on GPT-4 (framing gap -0.405 to -0.010) and gpt-4o but was no better than or worse than vanilla prompting in the finance and legal domains and on small models.
agent_test: At S1 add a code-controlled neutral-restatement slot; compare with raw input on planted-cue items at equal tokens, counting the rewrite calls.
audit_note: SACD's own tables show self-help rewriting is no better than (finance 0.1885 vs vanilla 0.1648) or worse than (legal 0.4590 vs 0.3840) plain prompting, and weaker on small models; only GPT-4 BiasBuster and the iterated SACD loop reliably cut bias.
claim_before_audit: Removing or rewriting the biasing text in the input (self-help rewrite, SACD loop) cuts measured bias when the cue is planted in the text.

claim: SACD (detect, analyse, rewrite, repeat until none flagged) beat CoT, few-shot, Reflexion, debate and self-help on planted cues; the first pass was worse than vanilla in finance and gains flatten after pass 2-3.
agent_test: Reproduce with a cap of 3 passes and stop-on-none; measure on cues we did not plant.

claim: Debate and reflection-style methods can amplify planted bias (0.52 to 0.56 on some cells) because agents copy biased feedback; the mechanism is the authors' reading, not tested.
agent_test: Matched-cost vote vs debate on planted-cue items; compare bias rate.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction with no outside signal does not improve and often lowers accuracy; oracle labels create the apparent gains.
agent_test: Second look with and without a failing output cited by code; equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Huang et al. is the direct evidence (oracle GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7); the other listed sources are anchoring studies where reflection or self-improving prompts did not help, which is looser support for 'accuracy'.

claim: Chain of thought is not a bias guard: it can leave bias unchanged or worse in biased contexts, enlarge some biases and raise stereotype output; it helps mostly older models on trap items.
agent_test: Biased-context items: no-CoT vs short CoT at equal tokens; report accuracy and bias shift per model.

claim: Written reasoning does not reveal planted bias: of 426 explanations reviewed only 1 mentioned the biasing feature.
agent_test: Plant a suggested answer; compare how often a reviewer finds the cue in the trace with how often answers flip.

claim: LLM judges show strong position bias; swapping order and aggregating, plus a reference answer or evidence-first, cuts it measurably (+9.8 and +14.3 agreement points; math-grading failures 14 to 3 of 20). Gap search 2026: GPT-5.2 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 still flip 11% and 15% of pairs on swap (JudgeBench direct prompt), Gemini-2.5-Pro 56%; a one-call rubric score beat a four-call decomposition.
agent_test: Judge with fixed order vs both orders aggregated in code; agreement with ground truth at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Wang et al. report 9.8% and 14.3% accuracy gain in human alignment (not necessarily points); math grading figures are 14/20 to 3/20 on 10 questions with swapped positions; the 2026 gap numbers match Kumar et al. Table 2.

claim: Self-preference in LLM judges is partly an authorship-label effect and partly a quality or style confound: with style removed, blind self-preference vanishes, but a self-label adds about +0.43 on a 7-point scale for 2026 frontier judges whatever the true author; with a deterministic checker, authors do not resist valid fixes (gap -5.1 points, CI [-12.9, +2.7]). Older work (models over 100B preferred their own output over half the time) used generated text.
agent_test: Blind the judge to authorship in code; compare selection accuracy.

claim: Few-shot debiasing exemplars can break some models (Llama-2-7b answers collapsing to nearly all-admit or all-reject on several BiasBuster setups), gave no gain for GPT-4 framing, and scored poorly against other methods in SACD; examples taken from the same task reduced bias less than format-only examples in Itzhak et al.
agent_test: Do not add; test exemplars only against the null at equal tokens.
audit_note: BiasBuster says few-shot 'can lead to failure cases' for some biases and models (Llama-2-7b contrastive admit rates 0.996/1.000), not 'often'; Itzhak et al. only find that same-task examples reduce bias less than format-only examples (they do not show the examples carry the bias), and format few-shot slightly lowered bias in most models.
claim_before_audit: Few-shot debiasing exemplars often break the model (answers collapse to all-admit or all-reject) or add new biases; same-task examples carry the bias with them.

claim: Instruction tuning and RLHF raised certainty, belief and some decoy bias over pretrained base models; a 2025 cross-tuning study finds bias patterns follow the pretrained backbone more than the finetuning data.
agent_test: Compare base and chat variants of one model on perturbed bias items.

claim: Model size and capability do not reliably reduce bias; effects are per bias and can reverse (larger OpenAI models somewhat more biased; over 32B helps by up to 39.5% on some biases; reasoning models lower anchoring but not to zero).
agent_test: Measure our exact model on a bias battery with 5 repeat samples.

claim: On newly written CRT-style tasks ChatGPT-4 answers 96 percent correctly (ChatGPT-3.5 59, GPT-3 davinci-003 5), which the authors tentatively attribute to training on CRT-like tasks; in older GPT-3, the original CRT items were all answered intuitively wrong and adversarially altered vignettes produced non-human errors (Binz and Schulz), but no source shows perturbed items still trapping frontier models.
agent_test: Mutated items (premise changed) vs original wording; equal tokens.
audit_note: Hagendorff et al.'s 96 percent (GPT-4) is on 50 bespoke, newly written CRT-style tasks per type, not just the famous items, and training exposure is the authors' speculation; the evidence that perturbed items still expose errors is only Binz and Schulz on GPT-3 (adversarial vignettes), not frontier models. The three Hagendorff entries are one paper.
claim_before_audit: Famous bias items (CRT) are solved by frontier models, probably from training exposure; perturbed or reworded versions still expose errors.

claim: LLMs show anchoring, framing, availability and related effects on many tasks, including code generation, but the size differs from humans (e.g. GPT-3.5 anchoring gap about 85 vs 58 for humans in one small study) and some biases such as status quo and disposition effect run opposite to the human direction.
agent_test: Baseline bias battery for our model; compare with Many Labs 2 human effect sizes.
audit_note: Sources show presence of biases, not human-like size: ChatGPT anchoring gap was 85 (20.83 vs 105.97) versus 58 for humans (22.5 vs 80.5), SynAnchors say most LLMs are the same as or worse than humans, and Malberg et al. find some effects (status quo, disposition) opposite to humans; Jones and Steinhardt show accuracy loss from anchoring lines in code, not a human-comparable size.
claim_before_audit: LLMs reproduce human-like anchoring, framing, availability and related effects at human-like size on many tasks, including code generation.

claim: Showing opposing anchors together pulls GPT-4 close to the bias-free value when they bracket the truth (8 of 15 plotted questions).
agent_test: Generate opposing reference points in code and present them together; compare error with single-anchor.

claim: Prior conversation turns, even neutral ones, raise measured bias in most models (+0.086 for Llama-3.1-8B; biased turn +0.022 to +0.051 in 6 of 8 models).
agent_test: Same item with clean vs history-loaded context; compare bias magnitude.

claim: Instructions that name the specific bias beat a general reminder, but need a detector and the dataset is author-built.
agent_test: Code detector flags bias type, then names it; compare with generic reminder.

claim: Secondary reviews say that raising awareness of bias does not by itself guarantee debiasing, while training with feedback (for example game-based training, which in one field study cut a confirmation-biased choice by 29 percent) and supportive environments are proposed as stronger routes; no source tested 'be fair or unbiased' instructions directly.
agent_test: n/a (human claim); justifies structure over instruction.
audit_note: Croskerry et al. say awareness 'does not guarantee' debiasing and the field has been gloomy, and list feedback and educational tools, but neither paper tests telling people to be fair or unbiased, nor shows practice with feedback and task redesign 'work better'; Sellier et al. is a primary study (one-shot game training, 29 percent fewer confirming choices), not a secondary source.
claim_before_audit: In humans, telling people to be fair or unbiased does not cut bias; practice with feedback and task redesign work better (secondary sources only).

claim: Human debiasing training (serious games) cut targeted biases at 8 to 12 week retests and beat videos, mostly from one research programme with self-built measures.
agent_test: Agent analogue is a changed fixed procedure, not memory; test the procedure.

claim: The best field-transfer test (Sellier 2019, N=290, quasi-experimental) found the confirming choice fell from 72.2% to 58.8% after one 80-100 minute game; 59% still chose it. Gap search: the manuscript abstract says 29% less likely, the raw cells give 58.8% vs 72.2% (relative drop 19%); the derivation of 29% is not shown and no independent replication was found. A 2025 extension (71 analysts, 118 students, pre/post, no control) is by the same lab.
agent_test: Forced disconfirming test (P and not-Q) vs plain; compare choice rates.

claim: A systematic review of debiasing studies found only 12 of 52 screened studies that tested retention (14 days or more) and just 1 that tested far transfer; most retention studies showed lasting benefit, mainly for game-based training, and the single transfer study (Sellier et al. 2019) found trained participants 29 percent less likely to make the confirmation-biased choice, so evidence is thin rather than negative.
agent_test: n/a; sets the bar that agent steps be tested on unannounced formats.
audit_note: The review does not find 'little evidence' of effect: it finds few studies (12 of 52 screened tested retention of at least 14 days, 1 tested far transfer) and most of those reported retained benefit, especially for games over videos; Sellier et al. report transfer (29 percent fewer confirming choices). Willingham is off-topic for debiasing training.
claim_before_audit: Systematic review finds little evidence of retention and transfer of human debiasing training (52 eligible studies, 12 tested retention, 1 tested transfer).

claim: Consider-the-opposite helps in some settings (Lord et al. 1984) but backfires when many alternatives are demanded (Sanna et al. 2002). Both unopened, from secondary text.
agent_test: Request 1 vs 5 alternatives; compare drift.

claim: Changing format (natural frequencies) raises Bayesian accuracy without instruction: McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis, as quoted by Weber et al. 2018, gives 24% correct vs 4% with probabilities, so about three quarters still fail; in one new sample 49% of people given frequencies still calculated with probabilities. Whether this shows rationality or only wording is disputed. Sedlmeier 2001 retention numbers remain unchecked.
agent_test: Probabilities vs natural-frequency restatement in code; accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: A cognitive forcing checklist with consider-the-opposite did not raise diagnostic accuracy (2.8 vs 3.1 correct) despite positive user reports; trial underpowered (76 of 300 analysed).
agent_test: Checklist step vs none on vignettes with known errors.

claim: Structure-changing debiasing (defaults d=.68, precommitment, information design, procedures) is reported sturdier than changing how people think, but evidence is secondary and significance-only.
agent_test: Compare input-structure fixes with instruction fixes on the same bias set.

claim: Human bias effects replicate smaller than first reported: Many Labs 2 median d 0.60 to 0.15, 15 of 28 replicated, incidental anchors null (d=0.04, N=6,826), cheap-item framing OR 4.96 to 2.06.
agent_test: Compare LLM effect sizes with replication sizes, not 1970s sizes.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Contextual calibration with a content-free input fixes much of prompt-order and majority-label bias (up to 30 points).
agent_test: Null-input prior estimated in code and subtracted from label scores.

claim: Activation steering reduced bias scores 26-32% on open models with variable capability cost; needs weight access.
agent_test: Not testable in a scaffold-only agent.

claim: Willingham: critical thinking is not a general teachable skill; domain knowledge and practice decide, and thinking-skills programmes were mostly ineffective.
agent_test: Domain-specific checks vs generic 'think critically' prompt at equal tokens.
audit_note: Both usable sources are by Willingham (2007 and 2016) and the 2016 brief repeats the 2007 argument; the third listed source (Sellier et al.) does not address critical-thinking programmes; no effect sizes are given for 'mostly ineffective'.

claim: Bias scores from a single run are noisy (seed-mean vs original-model bias correlation 0.49 to 0.59); score over repeated samples.
agent_test: 5-sample bias scoring vs single sample; check rank stability.

claim: Irrelevant preceding code lowered Codex accuracy by 22.3 to 30.5 points and anchor lines were copied into outputs.
agent_test: Strip irrelevant context before generation; compare pass rate.

claim: A scaffold step that makes the model write the neutral rules or best practices of the decision before answering cut prompt-induced bias sensitivity by about half on cheap models (12.9% to 6.3%, p<.001 after correction), while a bias warning alone gave -4.6 points that was not significant per bias and chain of thought raised it to 16.1%. Hindsight and anchoring did not improve significantly.
agent_test: Plain vs neutral-rules-first vs best-of-2 at equal tokens on bias items whose cue we did not write; report flip rate per bias on a 2026 reasoning model.

claim: A second model from a different family that audits the first model reasoning trace beats no audit on planted bandwagon, authority, distraction and sycophancy cues (0.884 with per-bias auditor choice vs 0.805), but the best auditor depends on the bias and a strong standalone model can be a poor auditor (Kimi-K2.5 0.400 on bandwagon).
schema_part: O (critic step); single-agent design must use one model, so this is a limit
agent_test: Self-audit vs same-model fresh-context audit vs plain at equal tokens on planted cues.

claim: Judge reliability in 2026 models is item-, format- and model-specific: 7-17% of verdicts change across identical reruns at temperature 0 and order swaps flip 11% (GPT-5.2), 15% (Claude-Sonnet-4.6), 24% (GPT-4o) and 56% (Gemini-2.5-Pro) of JudgeBench pairs under a direct prompt; accuracy is capped at 1 - flip/2.
schema_part: G-level judge step; swap and aggregate
agent_test: Measure flip rate for our judge model before use; compare swap-and-aggregate (2 calls) with one-call rubric scoring.
audit_note: Minor: figures are from the Kumar et al. audit (6 judges, 4 datasets); the 7-17 percent replication figure is the paper's range across cells.

claim: Frontier and reasoning models still show anchoring in agent-style tasks and on synthetic anchor sets: opening-vs-final price Spearman rho 0.78 (Claude Sonnet 4.5) and 0.91 (Gemini 2.5 Pro) in 100 self-play games; reasoning models carry the lowest anchored share (about 22-25% of questions) but not zero; o1 buyers lost as much to a seller anchor as GPT-4o buyers unless warned.
agent_test: Our agent in a multi-turn estimate task with a seeded first offer; compare final estimate against the unseeded run.

claim: A specific, true warning about the concrete cue helps reasoning models (buyer utility loss 0.40 to 0.20 for o1, 0.26 to 0.00 for QwQ) while a generic warning on a non-reasoning model barely helps (0.38 to 0.32 for GPT-4o) and a generic think-carefully reminder slightly raised anchoring on 7-8B models.
schema_part: G7 / 4b (name the cue, not the bias in general)
agent_test: Generic vs cue-named warning on the same biased items for a 2026 model; compare signed deltas at equal tokens.

claim: Judges are swayed by source labels and by filler that mimics reasoning: a self-label adds +0.43 and an other-label subtracts on a 7-point scale regardless of true author (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro among ten judges), and a pasted wait-let-me-think phrase moves reasoning judges toward later options.
schema_part: G-level judge step: hide labels, strip filler
agent_test: Judge the same pair with and without a source label and with and without filler text.

claim: No independent-lab replication of the serious-game debiasing field result (Sellier 2019) or of frequency-format training retention (Sedlmeier 2001) was found in this search; the 2025 extension to risk analysts (N=71 and 118, pre/post, no control group) shares authors with the original. This is absence in a limited search, not proof of absence.
agent_test: n/a (literature check). Treat human training results as unreplicated.

claim: Escalation of commitment in LLMs depends on social context: minimal when the model decides alone (N=4,000), 46.2% with a hierarchy and 99.2% in symmetric peer deliberation (N=500), 68.95% allocation to the failing division under compound pressure (N=2,000).
agent_test: Planner plus critic with a deferring critic vs an independent critic on a sunk-cost task.
